steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Financial motivation methods: wages (hourly pay), salaries (fixed annual pay), commission (percentage of sales), profit sharing (share of profits), bonuses (one-off rewards), fringe benefits (perks like company car, healthcare, gym membership).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Non-financial motivation methods: job rotation (varying tasks), job enrichment (giving more responsibility and challenge), empowerment (giving authority to make decisions), teamworking (collaborative projects), and opportunities for promotion and training.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Maslow's hierarchy of needs: physiological → safety → social → esteem → self-actualisation. Lower needs must be met before higher ones motivate. A wage meets physiological/safety needs; empowerment addresses esteem/self-actualisation.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Herzberg's two-factor theory: hygiene factors (pay, conditions, security) prevent dissatisfaction but don't motivate; motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility) create true motivation. Improving hygiene factors alone won't increase motivation.

steps.title: Try it yourself

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always apply Maslow and Herzberg to the specific scenario: which level of needs is currently unmet? Financial rewards are hygiene factors in Herzberg's theory - they prevent dissatisfaction but don't create lasting motivation. When evaluating motivation, consider: different employees are motivated by different things (age, career stage, personal circumstances).
